top: Mitochondrial and cellular energy starvation is what you get when there's not enough of the fuels each type of cell in your gut prefers (glutamine and butyrate). Your gut barrier needs a lot of energy, to keep its tight junctions intact. If the cells lining your small intestine (called enterocytes) or the colonocytes lining your large intestine don't do that, the barrier loosens up. Then lipopolysaccharides (LPS, which come from the walls of bacteria) and other endotoxins leak through those (not-so-tight)-junction gaps into your bloodstream.
glutamine: L-Glutamine ([watch Dr. Rhonda vid](https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=5DVUEKrekYw&ra=m)) is the main fuel for your enterocytes, and for your immune cells when they're activated. It doesn't have to go through the complicated digestive steps other nutrients do. Inside the mitochondria, it gets turned straight into alpha-ketoglutarate, or α-KG. The α-KG goes into the citric acid cycle, which is how the mitochondria make their energy. So that's why consuming pure glutamine gives energy to those cells faster than eating food. They then use their extra energy to repair the gut lining by pulling the tight junctions together, and that keeps LPS from getting through. Glutamine also provides nitrogen to help build new cells.
dosing: Take 5g a day as a baseline. The point of that baseline is to counter the breakdown of the gut lining that high-intensity or high-volume training causes, like CrossFit or intense cardio. If your immune system is dealing with an acute exposure, if your whole system is under a lot of stress, or if you have active IBD (Crohn's or colitis), raise it gradually to 10-30g a day.
caution: CAUTION: cancer cells that multiply really fast can grab glutamine too, to fuel their growth. So if you have an active colon or liver cancer, don't raise the dose that high. The liver is on that list because it's where the glutamine goes first, through the portal vein.
butyrate: The colonocytes lining your large intestine are fueled by short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) like butyrate, while your small intestine runs on glutamine. Your gut bacteria make SCFAs when they ferment raw resistant starch, and you get SCFAs directly from your home-brewed SIBO yogurt too. Besides feeding the colonocytes, SCFAs lock down the barrier in your lower gut, preventing the dangerous escape of substances from gut to blood, which then turns down inflammatory signals that would be needed otherwise to contain the damage.
tca_before: TCA cycle intermediates, like malic and citric acid, are organic acids that go directly into the same energy pathways in the mitochondria that glutamine does. So clean sour stuff like organic malic acid, tart cherries or green apples gives the cells lining your gut another quick fuel, and it speeds up healing of the lining, just by a different biochemical route than glutamine.
acids: Malic and citric acid (which make green apples and tart cherries sour) are made and used partway round that same cycle, also called the TCA or Krebs cycle, so in theory they're a quick energy source for your enterocytes too. But nobody has shown that eating them gives those cells much extra fuel on top of the glutamine. They do help you absorb iron, though. In one study, people absorbed two to three times as much of the iron in a rice meal when 1 g of pure malic or citric acid was mixed in ([Gillooly et al., 1983](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/6860621/)), probably because the acids help keep the iron dissolved so the gut can take it up. So something sour with an iron-rich meal is worth having anyway.
his_tca: Malic and citric acid (which make green apples and tart cherries sour) are quick energy sources for the lining cells of your small intestines. That's because they are intermediate products in the cells' mitochondrial energy production cycle, called TCA, Krebs, or citric acid cycle. Glutamine also fuels that same cycle via a different route, as it converts to a-KG, while also providing nitrogen to help build new cells. Those lining cells then use the energy they get from those fuels to heal the gut lining by pulling the tight junctions together.
tca_r04: Malic and citric acid are what's called TCA cycle intermediates. TCA is another name for the citric acid cycle, the one the glutamine ends up in, and these acids are already part of it, so your mitochondria can use them for energy directly. They're the acids that make green apples and tart cherries sour, so eating clean sour stuff like that, or taking organic malic acid, gets the cells lining your gut another fuel, and quickly. Glutamine has to be turned into α-KG first, so that's a different biochemical route, but either way those cells then use the extra energy to heal the gut lining faster.
acids_v1: Malic and citric acid (which make green apples and tart cherries sour) are intermediate products in that same cycle, also called the TCA or Krebs cycle, so in theory they're a quick energy source for those lining cells too. But there's no good evidence they add much next to glutamine. The better reason to eat them is iron: in one study, adding 1 g of malic or citric acid to a rice meal raised how much of its iron people absorbed two to three times ([Gillooly et al., 1983](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/6860621/)).
acids_v2: Malic and citric acid (which make green apples and tart cherries sour) are made and used partway round that same cycle, also called the TCA or Krebs cycle, so in theory they're a quick energy source for your enterocytes too. But there's no good evidence they add much fuel on top of what glutamine gives. The better reason to eat them is iron: they help keep the iron in a meal dissolved, so more of it gets absorbed. In one study, adding 1 g of pure malic or citric acid to a rice meal raised how much of its iron people absorbed two to three times, and the vegetables whose iron was well absorbed had a good amount of these acids in them ([Gillooly et al., 1983](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/6860621/)).
acids_v3: Malic and citric acid (which make green apples and tart cherries sour) are made and used partway round that same cycle, also called the TCA or Krebs cycle, so in theory they're a quick energy source for your enterocytes too. But nobody has shown that eating them adds much to the fuel the glutamine already gives those cells. Where they do help is with iron, because they help keep the iron in your food dissolved so your gut can absorb it. In one study, people absorbed two to three times as much of the iron in a rice meal when 1 g of pure malic or citric acid was added to it, and the vegetables whose iron was absorbed well had a good amount of these acids in them ([Gillooly et al., 1983](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/6860621/)).
